title: The Problem with Prioritization Matrices
excerpt: RICE, ICE, WSJF, Kano — the frameworks are everywhere. But most teams use them to defer hard conversations, not make better decisions.
content:
If you have attended a product management meetup in the last five years, you have seen the slide. A 2x2 grid. Value on one axis, effort on the other. Dots scattered across quadrants. The presenter says something like "this is how we prioritize" and the room nods.

It feels rigorous. It looks data-driven. It is almost always doing less work than it pretends to.

Why Prioritization Matrices Feel Safe

A matrix gives a team the sensation of having thought through its choices. You have scored each initiative. You have plotted them. You have a visual that says "we did the work." For engineering teams under pressure to justify what they are building, that visual is a shield — it transforms a judgment call into a process output.

The problem is that the inputs to the matrix are almost never as objective as the output suggests.

The Scoring Trap

Take RICE: Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort. Each initiative gets a score, and the highest scores rise to the top. Clean, right?

The catch is in the word Confidence. It is the escape hatch teams use when they do not actually know what they are scoring. A feature with vague impact gets a low confidence multiplier. A feature the team is excited about gets a high one. The matrix has not resolved uncertainty — it has just buried it inside a formula and called the result a number.

And the numbers are almost always relative, even when presented as absolute. "Impact: 3 out of 5" means whatever the person holding the scoring rubric wants it to mean. Two PMs at the same company will score the same initiative differently because they weight customer requests, strategic alignment, and engineering opinion differently. The matrix makes disagreement invisible.

What Matrices Are Good At

None of this means matrices are useless. They are genuinely helpful for:

  • Surface-level sequencing — if you have ten items that are all roughly comparable and you need a starting point for discussion, a matrix gives you a defensible first draft.
  • Spotting imbalances — a grid can reveal that everything is "high effort, low value" or that the team has no stretch bets at all. That pattern is worth a conversation.
  • Aligning vocabulary — when a team agrees that "effort" means "engineering weeks including QA," the matrix becomes a shared language instead of a each-person-uses-their-own-definition mess.

These are real benefits. But they are conversation starters, not decision engines.

What They Hide

The work a matrix cannot capture is the work that actually decides outcomes:

  • Dependencies — a low-score item that unblocks three higher-score items is not low-priority. The matrix has no place for this unless you add another layer of scoring, at which point you are scoring the scoring.
  • Strategic forcing functions — sometimes you build something not because the ROI is obvious today but because it opens a door that closes otherwise. A matrix scores the door, not the fact that it locks forever at the end of the quarter.
  • Customer trust — a promised feature that five major customers are waiting on may score low on reach and impact today and still need to move up. Matrices are bad at urgency that comes from relationships, not metrics.
  • Opportunity cost of delay — doing nothing also has a cost, and most matrices treat the status quo as a neutral baseline instead of a decaying asset.

A Better Use

The healthiest teams I have worked with treat prioritization matrices as artifacts of the conversation, not substitutes for it. They use the grid in the room, on a whiteboard, with the people who will do the work. They argue about the scores. They change them when someone raises a dependency nobody had named. The final plot is not a verdict — it is a summary of a discussion that already happened.

The unhealthy version is the one that ships to a slide deck, gets forwarded to a stakeholder who was not in the room, and becomes the justification for a decision nobody is allowed to revisit.

Matrices are not the problem. The problem is using them to avoid the thing they cannot do: weigh judgment, context, and timing against each other when the numbers do not tell the whole story.

If your prioritization framework would still give you the same answer in the dark, with no grid in front of you, it is probably adding value. If it would not, you are not prioritizing — you are formatting.
